title: Story: how to be happy
summary: The story of Heinrich, an old farmer who carries two invisible baskets; Maria teaches him to let go of the bad things. Told in the Präteritum, with polite Sie conversation and Konjunktiv II.
phrases: Once upon a time there was an old farmer.
He carries something around with him.
I can manage on my own.
May I come in for a moment?
You don't have to forget. You only have to let go.
I don't carry that any more.
In the past he would have carried that around for days.
phraseNotes: etw. mit sich herumtragen = to carry inside
lines: Once upon a time there was an old farmer called Heinrich, who lived at the edge of a small village.
His house stood a little apart, surrounded by a modest vegetable field that he worked every day with tired but hard-working hands.
Heinrich had not always been alone.
His wife had died many years ago, and since then he had lived a withdrawn life in his little house.
Every morning he got up early, even before the sun had properly risen.
He worked in his field, harvested potatoes, cabbage and carrots, and then went to the village market to sell his vegetables.
The villagers knew Heinrich as a quiet, serious man.
In the past, the older ones remembered, he had smiled, greeted people cheerfully and sometimes even joked.
But over the years something in him had grown heavy.
His face looked careworn.
His eyes were often fixed on the ground, and his shoulders seemed to sag under an invisible load.
When someone spoke to him at the market, he answered briefly and curtly, sometimes even gruffly.
Some people said: "Heinrich has just got old."
Others whispered: "He carries something around with him that won't let him go."
They were right without knowing it.
Heinrich carried something with him: two invisible baskets.
Nobody could see them, but he felt their weight every single day.
One basket was meant for the good things: a kind word, a rich harvest, a warm sunbeam, an honest smile.
This basket was small and light, almost empty.
Heinrich hardly paid any attention to it.
The other basket was big and heavy.
In it Heinrich collected everything that had ever hurt, disappointed or offended him.
And he collected carefully.
Ten years ago a neighbour hadn't told him the whole truth when a field was sold.
That lay deep down in the basket.
Five years ago a rich woman at the market had laughed when he was forced to offer a lower price.
He had put that in too, carefully and firmly.
Three years ago a young man had said to him in passing: "Those trousers look old."
And Heinrich had put those words into the basket like a stone.
Every time someone overlooked him, every time a customer went to another stall, every time he felt lonely or forgotten – all of it collected in the heavy basket.
And Heinrich carried it with him everywhere.
One day – it was a mild autumn day – Heinrich sat on an old wooden bench in the market square and watched the people around him.
He had already sold his vegetables – not much, but enough for a few days.
A young trader laughed loudly with his customers and gave a child a little carrot.
An old woman shared her bread with a beggar.
Two men helped each other lift heavy sacks onto a cart.
Heinrich saw all of it, but he felt nothing but bitterness.
"They have it easy," he thought, and frowned.
"They don't know what it's like to be alone. They weren't cheated, forgotten, hurt like me."
He stood up slowly, his knees creaking, and went back to his house at the edge of the village.
Every step felt heavy, as if he were carrying a huge sack on his back.
And that is exactly what he was doing – invisible to others, but completely real to him.
The basket with all the bad memories pressed on his shoulders, on his heart, on his soul.
That evening Heinrich sat in his small dark kitchen and silently ate his simple meal: bread, some cheese, a few boiled potatoes.
He thought about the day, the years, all the times life had hurt him.
With every thought the basket got a little heavier.
He didn't know it, but he was feeding his own burden – thought by thought, memory by memory, hurt by hurt.
Outside the sun slowly went down, and darkness settled gently over the little village.
In Heinrich's heart it had been dark for a long time.
The days passed, and Heinrich's burden grew heavier and heavier.
He hardly spoke to the neighbours any more, and when he did, only what was necessary.
At the market he set out his vegetables in silence, took the money and left again.
People began to avoid him.
"He's become so grumpy," they said. "You can't talk to him any more."
Heinrich noticed that too and put it in the basket.
One morning, just as he was watering his field, a young woman came along the path.
It was Maria, his neighbour, who lived a little further on in the village.
She was friendly and helpful, always with a smile on her lips.
Maria was carrying a basket of fresh bread.
"Good morning, Mr Heinrich!" she called cheerfully.
Heinrich glanced up briefly and gave a curt nod, without smiling.
Maria came closer. "I baked too much bread today. Would you like some?"
"No, thank you," said Heinrich gruffly, and turned away.
"Are you sure? It's still warm …"
"I don't need anything," he interrupted her. "I can manage on my own."
Maria stood still for a moment, then nodded gently.
"If you change your mind – I'm just over there."
She walked away, and Heinrich was left alone.
Instead of relief he felt a strange heaviness.
"She only wants to help me out of pity," he thought. "She thinks I'm a poor, lonely old man."
And he put that in the basket too.
A few days later they met again at the market.
Maria was buying vegetables from another trader, a young, friendly man who laughed loudly and made jokes.
Heinrich saw it and felt a sting.
"Of course," he muttered to himself. "She doesn't come to me. Why would she?"
He packed up his things and went home earlier than usual.
On the way he stopped, suddenly out of breath.
His heart was beating heavily, his legs felt as heavy as lead.
He sat down on a stone by the roadside and took a deep breath.
"What's wrong with me?" he whispered.
But he knew. The basket had become too heavy.
All the years, all the hurts, all the bitterness – they were slowly crushing him.
The next day Maria came to his house again. This time she brought nothing with her.
She knocked on the door, and after a long pause Heinrich opened it.
"What do you want?" he asked curtly.
"I just wanted to see how you are," Maria said calmly. "You were so pale yesterday."
Heinrich said nothing.
"May I come in for a moment?" she asked carefully.
He hesitated, then stepped aside.
They sat down at the little kitchen table. For a while they sat there in silence.
Then Maria said quietly: "Heinrich … what makes you so heavy?"
He looked at her in surprise. "Who … me?"
"Yes," she said gently. "I can see it. You carry something around with you that you can't let go."
Heinrich pressed his lips together. "That's none of your business."
"Maybe not," Maria admitted. "But I can see how it's eating you up, and that hurts me."
"Why?" he asked hoarsely. "Why do you care?"
"Because I saw my grandfather just like this," Maria said quietly. "He was like you.
He remembered every hurt, every loss, every injustice. He carried it all around with him – for years."
Heinrich swallowed. For the first time in a long while he felt that someone understood him.
"What happened to him?" he asked after a pause.
Maria smiled gently. "He found an answer. But only when it had almost broken him."
"What kind of answer?" Heinrich's voice sounded hoarse.
"He told me a story," said Maria, "about two baskets that every person carries."
Heinrich flinched. "Two baskets?"
"Yes." Maria looked him in the eyes. "Do you know the feeling?"
He nodded slowly, unable to speak. His breathing was heavy.
"May I tell you what my grandfather learned?" Maria asked gently.
Heinrich sat still for a long time. Part of him wanted to throw her out and stay alone with his bitterness.
But another part, a small, quiet part, wanted to listen.
Then, almost against his will, he nodded.
"Come," said Maria. "Let's walk a little. Fresh air does you good."
They got up and slowly went outside. The sun was high in the sky, and a gentle wind blew across the fields.
Heinrich walked beside Maria, silent, waiting.
Part of him wanted to run away, but another part stayed.
"Maybe," he thought carefully, "maybe there really is an answer."
He hardly dared to believe it.
They walked slowly along the field path, past the golden wheat fields and old fruit trees.
Maria was silent for a while, as if looking for the right words. At last she began to speak quietly.
"My grandfather was a proud man," she said. "He worked hard, loved his family, helped his neighbours.
But he had one weakness: he couldn't forget. Every injustice, every disappointment, every harsh word – he kept it all."
Heinrich nodded silently. He understood that only too well.
"Over the years he became bitter," Maria went on. "Just like you.
He didn't speak much any more, he didn't smile any more. People said his heart had grown hard."
"And then?" Heinrich asked quietly.
Maria smiled gently. "One day he was sitting under an old tree, exhausted by his burden.
A wanderer came by, a wise old man with kind eyes. He sat down beside my grandfather and asked:
'Why do you carry two baskets, my friend?'
My grandfather was confused. 'What baskets?' he asked.
The wanderer smiled. 'Everyone carries two invisible baskets through life. One for the good things, one for the bad.'
'But most people make a mistake. They keep the basket for the bad firmly shut so that nothing falls out.
The basket for the good they leave open, and everything simply falls out and is lost.'
Heinrich stopped. His hands were trembling slightly.
Maria looked at him. "The wanderer showed my grandfather something. He took two small woven baskets out of his bag.
One was tightly woven, without holes. The other had big gaps, little openings everywhere.
'This is how it should be,' said the wanderer. 'Hold on tight to the basket for the good. Close it well so nothing is lost.
But the basket for the bad – give it holes. Let the bad things fall out by themselves as you walk on.'
'But that's unfair!' my grandfather cried. 'The people who hurt me, should they just get away with it?'
The wanderer shook his head. 'No, my friend. It isn't about them getting away with it. It's about you becoming free.
If you hold on to the burden, you carry it – not them. You are the prisoner.'"
Heinrich was breathing heavily. His eyes were burning.
"My grandfather didn't understand it straight away," Maria said quietly. "He asked: 'How am I supposed to do that? I can't just forget.'
The wanderer smiled gently. 'You don't have to forget. You only have to let go.
Every time a bad memory rises in you, imagine it falling through the holes in your basket. You don't carry it any more. You leave it behind on the path.'"
They walked on, and Maria spoke more quietly.
"It took weeks. My grandfather practised every day.
When someone hurt him, he thought: 'That falls through the holes.' When he remembered old hurts, he told himself: 'I don't carry that any more.'"
"And?" Heinrich asked in a hoarse voice. "Did it work?"
Maria stopped and looked him in the eyes. "Yes. Slowly he became lighter. His face relaxed. He began to smile again.
Not because life was suddenly perfect, but because he stopped holding on to everything bad."
Heinrich stood still. The wind brushed gently over the fields.
Something was fighting inside him: the wish to let go and the fear of giving up his bitterness.
"But … if I let go," he whispered, "what will be left of me?"
Maria gently laid her hand on his arm.
"What really matters, Mr Heinrich. Your good heart, your strength, your life – everything that lies buried under the burden."
Heinrich closed his eyes. Tears ran down his old, weather-beaten cheeks.
"It hurts so much," he said quietly.
"I know," said Maria gently. "But do you know what hurts even more? Carrying the burden for ever."
They stood there in silence for a long time. Then Heinrich nodded slowly, very slowly.
"Holes," he whispered. "I need holes in my basket."
Maria smiled, and there was a warm glow in her eyes. "Yes. And you can start today."
In the weeks that followed, Heinrich tried to do what Maria had told him. It wasn't easy.
Every morning when he woke up, he felt the familiar weight on his chest – all the old memories.
But now he did something new: he imagined his basket for the bad getting holes. Big ones, small ones, everywhere.
One day at the market another trader sold his potatoes for less money.
In the past Heinrich would have carried that around with him for days: "Unfair! He's taking my customers away."
But this time he took a deep breath and thought: "That falls through the holes. I'm not carrying it."
It felt strange. Almost wrong, but also … lighter.
Another time a woman walked past his stall without noticing him.
The old pain rose up in him: overlooked again, forgotten again.
Then he closed his eyes for a moment and let it go. "Through the holes," he whispered. "I don't carry that any more."
Slowly, very slowly, something in him began to change.
One morning he got up and noticed that his shoulders weren't so heavy any more.
He went to the market, and for the first time in years he smiled at a child who passed his stall.
The child smiled back, and Heinrich felt a small, warm joy in his heart.
"That belongs in the other basket," he thought in amazement. "The one without holes."
Weeks passed. Heinrich kept practising. Sometimes he did well, sometimes he fell back into old patterns.
But every time he noticed he was collecting something heavy again, he remembered Maria's words, the wanderer, the holes in the basket.
One afternoon Maria came to see him again. This time she brought apples from her garden.
"Hello, Heinrich," she said warmly.
This time he smiled at her. "Good afternoon, Maria. Thank you for the apples. That's very kind of you."
Maria looked at him in surprise. Then she smiled warmly. "You look different," she said quietly.
"Different?"
"Lighter. As if you had put something down."
Heinrich nodded slowly. "I'm trying. It isn't always easy, but … I'm trying to have the basket with holes."
"That's all that matters," Maria said gently, "that you try."
They sat together in front of his house for a while, ate apples and talked about the harvest, the weather, the little things in life.
It was a simple conversation, but to Heinrich it felt like a gift.
When Maria left, Heinrich stayed sitting for a while. The sun slowly went down, and the sky turned red and gold.
He thought of all the years he had spent with his burden, of all the days he had lived in bitterness.
"What a waste," he whispered.
But this time it wasn't a reproachful thought, just a quiet realisation.
He got up and went into his house. For the first time in a long while he didn't feel alone.
Friends, this story teaches us something important.
We all carry two baskets through life: one for the good things, one for the bad.
Often we hold on to the bad things as if they were precious – every pain, every hurt, every disappointment.
We carry them with us, day after day, year after year, until they crush us.
But true happiness begins the moment we learn to let go. Not to forget, but to stop holding on.
Imagine your basket for the bad had holes. The burden would fall out by itself as you walk on. You wouldn't have to carry it any more.
That's not weakness. It's freedom.
Because every bad thing you let go of makes room for something good: for gratitude, for peace, for small, warm moments of joy.
A single thought can change everything: "I don't carry that any more."
Maybe today is the day you start making holes in your basket.
topics: Retell the story: who is Heinrich, what does he carry, how does it end?
Letting go: what is hard to let go of, and why does it help?
Happiness and gratitude: what are you grateful for?
A neighbour helps: how does Maria help Heinrich?

focus.title: Simple past (the storytelling tense)
points: Fairy tales and written texts are told in the Präteritum: Er lebte, er arbeitete, er ging
Regular verbs take -te: leben → lebte · sammeln → sammelte · arbeiten → arbeitete
Irregular verbs change their stem and must be learned: stehen → stand · tragen → trug · sitzen → saß · liegen → lag
With ich and er/sie/es the form is the same, no ending: ich trug = er trug

focus.title: Past perfect
points: For something that happened before the time of the story: hatte/war + Partizip II
Seine Frau war gestorben. — his wife had died (earlier)
Ein Nachbar hatte ihm nicht die volle Wahrheit gesagt.
Same rule as the Perfekt: verbs of movement and change of state with war, the rest with hatte

focus.title: As if … / if … (unreal)
points: als würde + Infinitiv = as if: als würde er einen Sack tragen
als hätten Sie etwas abgelegt = as if you had put something down · als wären sie kostbar
Unreal past: Früher hätte er das tagelang mit sich herumgetragen. (he would have, but not now)
Imagining: Stellt euch vor, euer Korb hätte Löcher. Ihr müsstet sie nicht mehr tragen.

focus.title: Relative clauses (who / which …)
points: The relative pronoun takes the gender and number of the noun before it, and the verb goes to the end: ein Bauer, der am Rand eines Dorfes lebte
Maria, die ein Stück weiter wohnte · ein Kind, das vorbeikam
Its case depends on its role in the clause: ein Feld, das er bearbeitete (Akkusativ)
After alles / das use was: alles, was ihn verletzt hatte · das, was wirklich zählt

focus.title: Separable verbs
points: In a main clause the prefix goes to the end: Er lässt los. · Er trägt etwas mit sich herum. · Sie ging davon.
In a subordinate clause the whole verb is at the end: wenn du weitergehst · damit nichts herausfällt
With zu, zu goes in the middle: loszulassen · festzuhalten · aufzugeben
In the participle, ge goes in the middle: herumgetragen · abgelegt · hineingelegt

focus.title: Polite Sie
points: Maria and Heinrich address each other with Sie: Wie geht es Ihnen? · Möchten Sie etwas davon haben?
Polite request: Darf ich einen Moment hereinkommen?
Polite imperative: Kommen Sie! · Lassen Sie uns ein Stück gehen.
The wanderer in the tale says du (friendly): Warum trägst du zwei Körbe, mein Freund?
